https://www.vol.at/police-stop-car-chase.text: APA/HARALD SCHNEIDER Nach einer spektakulären Verfolgungsjagd quer durch Wien hat die Polizei einen flüchtigen Autofahrer in Simmering gestoppt. Die Beamten schossen auf die Reifen des Wagens, um die Flucht zu beenden. Anzeige Anzeige The Vienna police ended a car chase on Wednesday, initiated by the driver of a car registered in Hungary, in Simmering by shooting one or more shots into the car tires. The driver was arrested. The man had caused a traffic accident with his car on Jedleseer Straße in Floridsdorf. When he noticed the police approaching, he fled. Multiple Accidents Caused During Escape Pursued by the authorities, the man sped over the Nordbrücke onto the A22 (Danube Bank Motorway) heading south. Through the Kaisermühlen Tunnel, he continued onto the A23 (Southeast Tangent) heading south and at the Danube Canal onto the A4 (East Motorway) heading out of the city. According to police spokesman Philipp Haßlinger, the driver caused several traffic accidents in the process. At the Alt-Simmering exit, the officers stopped him and shot his tires to make further escape impossible. The driver was arrested and is being charged with resisting state authority as well as other offenses. It initially remained unclear why the man fled. It cannot be ruled out and is the subject of further investigations that he might have committed other offenses and therefore sped away. Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Smoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid International airport in Riyadh on Saturday after missile and drone strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Photograph: Reuters US-Israel war on Iran Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels Patrick Wintour in New York Sun 20 Sep 2026 14.56 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic. In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East. Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”. The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”. Map indicating territory under de facto Houthi authority as of 11 September Iran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks. The outburst of sabre rattling appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels . The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attack since the Saudi Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted. The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies. Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies when he spurned a call by the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help. The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthis suddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coast overlooking the Red Sea , giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia. On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages. In a bid to keep the US out of its war with Saudi Arabia , the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that it would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, an undertaking that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily. Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise. Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.” The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September. Trump is due to meet the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council when he attends the UN general assembly in New York, in a meeting that is likely to cover Iran, Yemen, Gaza and the future of the US security guarantee. Trump said he was also open to a meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York, an encounter that would probably be rejected by the Iranians, who refuse to negotiate directly with the US, operating instead largely through mediators. Pezeshkian is one of many world leaders due to address a general assembly that is likely to be dominated, on the sidelines at least, by Trump’s Middle East crisis. In the first sign of a potential change of White House thinking about renewing US military action, the state department issued a security alert on Saturday to US citizens across the region warning “the security environment remains complex with potential for unforeseen escalation. American citizens in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance.” Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, said the attacks on Riyadh are a response to “hundreds of airstrikes that Riyadh had carried out against the people of Yemen”. In a lengthy statement to parliament on Sunday, Mohammad Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, insisted that Iran was not interested in waging a forever war with the US. But the new secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, a hardliner, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s seven preconditions for peace – which include the US lifting its blockade of Iran oil ports, the restoration of its frozen assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – remained. Rezaei also expressed his anger with the Gulf states, saying they had been invited to a meeting in Salahah in Oman last week to approve the agreed Oman-Iran plan for a new authorised shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, but Saudi Arabia rejected attendance. He said: “We invited them to the Salahah meeting and they reciprocated with a secret meeting in Germany with US Central Command and Israel.” Despite the Houthi victories last week, forces allied to the UN-recognised government of Yemen claimed to be pushing back against the Houthis across the country with 75 Houthi soldiers killed on Saturday alone. https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-donal.text: LONDON — The long-delayed deal over the future of the Chagos Islands is being reviewed by the British government after Donald Trump criticized it as "terrible." Defense Secretary Wes Streeting pledged Wednesday to work with the Trump administration to land an agreement over the Archipelago, which is home to the sensitive U.S. military base, Diego Garcia. Streeting told Times Radio that the government would not ignore Trump's grievances with the deal — cautioning that "sticking our heads in the sand and hoping it won't go away" is not "a wise strategy." Advertisement Advertisement Streeting's comments followed a meeting between Trump and Andy Burnham in which the U.S. president described the agreement brokered by Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer as "terrible." Under the most recent version of the plan — paused in April when Trump withdrew his support — Mauritius would gain sovereignty over the islands, which are one of Britain's last colonial possessions. The military base at Diego Garcia would be leased back to the U.K. and U.S. for a cost of £101m a year. Critics of the deal, including right-wing politicians in the U.K., argue that it risks allowing China a crucial toehold in a strategically-important region. Trump has said repeatedly that he wants permanent and unrestricted access to the military base — and re-iterated Tuesday that this is "strategically very important" for the U.S., especially in the context of its war with Iran. Streeting said that he had looked at the situation with a "fresh pair of eyes" after taking over the defense brief in July, and insisted the British "strategy is not to wait out President Trump." Working with the U.S. administration will be "difficult and necessarily painstaking work," he added. Advertisement Advertisement Burnham told reporters Wednesday that he would "work hard" to find a resolution that both the U.S. and U.K. could agree on. He added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well. "What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it." “It shouldn’t have taken another intervention from the president for Andy Burnham to ‘review’ Labour’s Chagos surrender deal,” argued Shadow Defence Secretary James Cartlidge Wednesday morning. The opposition rep added: “If Burnham was really serious about our defence he would know that this deal should be binned entirely. It is absurd to hand over British sovereign territory, not to mention billions of pounds of hard-pressed taxpayers’ money, to an ally of China.”

Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty US-Israel war on Iran Ed Miliband meets Iran’s foreign minister as Tehran gives US ultimatum on strait of Hormuz Senior Iranian officials say Washington has four to five days to respond to its conditions for reopening the strait Patrick Wintour in New York Thu 24 Sep 2026 15.13 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 15.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , has met his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, for the first time in New York amid warnings from senior Iranian security officials that the US has four to five days to respond to its conditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz. The previously unknown apparent deadline was specified by Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the supreme national security council, in a TV interview on Wednesday evening, and it is unclear what action Tehran will take if the US does not respond to Iran’s preconditions for reopening the vital waterway. A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday. Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk Read more Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond. Rezaei, a recently promoted hardliner, said Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Araghchi had flown to New York to convey Iran’s internally agreed terms, not to negotiate new ones. “There has been no discussion whatsoever that these conditions should change, that a new condition should be removed or added,” he said. The big change appears to be that Tehran now insists Washington act first. “Talk is enough. Negotiations are enough. Now we must act,” Rezaei said. He warned that if the US did “not fulfil the conditions, we will neither open the strait of Hormuz nor is there any negotiation on the table”. View image in fullscreen The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi (left), speaks with his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman Safadi, at the UN in New York. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Rezaei said the seven conditions must be implemented “completely and all at once”, adding that the US had been given “four or five days” to do so. After that, he said, Iran would determine its “next step”, without specifying what that would entail. The meeting between Miliband and Araghchi, one of an exhaustive round of bilaterals undertaken by the Iranian foreign minister, is the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries. Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen. He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran. Overall, European diplomats have not sensed a US-Iran breakthrough in New York. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, also said it would be wrong to characterise the Witkoff talks with Iran as a major breakthrough. It is understood that Araghchi, speaking largely through a Qatari mediator, set out to him the seven preconditions to be met before it is willing to reopen the strait, including the lifting of US sanctions and an end to war on all fronts, a reference to Israeli military activity in south Lebanon. Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis. Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.” Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks. He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases. Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.” Explore more on these topics US-Israel war on Iran Ed Miliband Iran Strait of Hormuz US foreign policy Trump administration US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
